'''''Thymus serpyllum''''', known by the common names of '''Breckland thyme''',<ref>Schauer, Thomas (1978). ''A Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain and Europe'', Collins, London, p. 184. {{ISBN|0-00-219257-8}}.</ref> '''Breckland wild thyme''', '''wild thyme''', '''creeping thyme''', or '''elfin thyme''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the mint family, [[Lamiaceae]]. It is a low, usually [[prostrate shrub|prostrate]] [[subshrub]] forming creeping stems up to {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} tall. The oval [[evergreen]] leaves are up to 8 mm. The strongly scented [[flower]]s are either lilac, pink-purple, or magenta, are up to 6 mm long and produced in clusters.

The species is [[Native species|native]] to most of Europe and North Africa. The hardy plant tolerates some pedestrian traffic and produces odors ranging from heavily herbal to lightly lemon, depending on the variety.

==Description==
Wild thyme is a creeping dwarf evergreen shrub, growing to {{Convert|10|cm|frac=4}} tall.<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=88}}</ref> It has woody stems up to 10 cm long and a [[taproot]]. It forms matlike plants that root from the nodes of the squarish, limp stems. The [[leaves]] are 3–8 mm long in opposite pairs, nearly stalkless, with linear elliptic round-tipped blades and untoothed margins. The plant sends up erect flowering shoots in summer. The flowers are 4–6 mm long and usually pink or mauve, rarely white, with a tube-like [[Sepal|calyx]] and an irregular straight-tubed, hairy [[corolla (flower)|corolla]]. The upper petal is notched and the lower one is larger than the two lateral petals and has three flattened lobes which form a lip. Each flower has four projecting stamens and two fused carpels. The fruit is a dry, four-chambered [[schizocarp]].<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web|url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/breckland-thyme|title=Breckland Thyme: ''Thymus serpyllum''|publisher=NatureGate|access-date=13 December 2013}}</ref>

=== Chemistry ===
The oils of ''T. serpyllum'' contain [[thymol]], [[carvacrol]], [[limonene]], [[paracymene]], [[gamma-terpinene]] and [[beta-caryophyllene]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Debaggio |first1=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7_KPgxEglHAC&q=thymol+%22thymus+quinquecostatus%22&pg=PA482 |title=The Encyclopedia of Herbs |last2=Tucker |first2=Arthur O. |date=2009 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=9781604691344 |page=482 |access-date=10 May 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Wild thyme is native to the [[Palearctic realm]] of Europe and Asia. It is a plant of thin soils and can be found growing on sandy-soiled heaths, rocky outcrops, hills, banks, roadsides and riverside sand banks.

== Ecology ==
Wild thyme is one of the plants on which both the [[common blue|common blue butterfly]] and [[large blue|large blue butterfly]] larvae feed and it is also attractive to bees.<ref name="NatureGate" /><ref>Eva Penn-Smith, [https://web.archive.org/web/20170701154613/http://butterfly-conservation.org/files/caterpillar-food-plants.pdf Caterpillar food plants] (PDF)</ref>

{{anchor|thyme lawn}}

==Cultivation==
Creeping and mounding variants of ''T. serpyllum'' are used as border plants and ground cover around gardens and stone paths. It may also be used to replace a [[Poa pratensis|bluegrass]] lawn to [[Xeriscaping|xeriscape]] low to moderate foot traffic areas due to its tolerance for low water and poor soils.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.finegardening.com/design/articles/thyme-the-fragrant-ground-cover.aspx|title=Thyme, the Fragrant Ground Cover|work=Fine Gardening|date=25 April 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardenguides.com/495-planting-maintiaining-thyme-lawn.html|title=Planting and Maintaining a Thyme Lawn|work=GardenGuides |date=13 June 2023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardenersgardening.com/xeriscape-dry-climate.html|title=What is Xeriscape Nothing More Than Seven Common Gardening Principals|access-date=23 May 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100515054837/http://www.gardenersgardening.com/xeriscape-dry-climate.html|archive-date=15 May 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Creeping thyme has also been used to "upholster" herb seats, similar to [[camomile seat]]s, and provide a fragrant surface to sit on.<ref>{{cite web |title=Let's be sitting pretty - A garden seat {{!}} a Kiwi Gardener project |url=https://www.resene.co.nz/Weekend-Gardener/Weekend-Gardener-51.htm |website=www.resene.co.nz |access-date=26 October 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Shallcross |first1=Marie |title=Midsummer Nights Dream Garden Design Inspiration |url=https://plewsgardendesign.co.uk/midsummer-nights-dream-garden-design-inspiration/ |website=Plews Garden Design |access-date=26 October 2024 |date=18 June 2023}}</ref>

Several [[cultivars]] have been produced, of which 'Pink Chintz' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Thymus serpyllum'' 'Pink Chintz'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/90194/Thymus-serpyllum-Pink-Chintz/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 102 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 23 December 2018}}</ref> A miniature creeping form is 'Elfin'.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardeningknowhow.com/edible/herbs/thyme/elfin-thyme-information.htm|title=Elfin Thyme Care – How Do I Plant Elfin Thyme In The Garden|work=Gardening Know How|date=April 2021 }}</ref>

==Uses==
Wild thyme can be used as a herb much as domestic [[thyme]], with a milder flavor.<ref name="tfb" />
